title: Crypto participation is retreating from its speculative peak while risk awareness remains high and unevenly distributed
source_unit: Gallup, U.S. Crypto Ownership Falls From 2025 High, September 21, 2026
geography: United States; adults and investors, with investors defined as those holding $10,000 or more in investable assets

observations.period: June 1-15, 2026 survey; ownership and participation funnel

denominator.unit: U.S. adults interviewed by web through Gallup's probability-based panel; more than 1,000 were investors

adult_ownership.unit: percent of U.S. adults reporting cryptocurrency ownership

adult_ownership_2025.unit: percent of U.S. adults reporting ownership in 2025

investor_ownership.unit: percent of U.S. investors reporting cryptocurrency ownership

investor_ownership_2025.unit: percent of U.S. investors reporting ownership in 2025

investor_ownership_decline.unit: percentage-point decline in investor ownership from 2025 to 2026

observations.method: Gallup June 1-15, 2026 probability-based web panel survey of 2,043 U.S. adults, including more than 1,000 investors defined as adults with at least $10,000 in investable assets.
observations.uncertainty: Ownership is self-reported and the investor subgroup has a smaller denominator; the survey does not measure holdings, gains, losses, transaction timing, debt, tax effects or financial suitability.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults overall and U.S. investors.
observations.counterinterpretation: The decline may reflect market-price changes, survey timing, portfolio reclassification, reduced salience or selling, rather than a durable rejection of crypto as a financial or cultural asset.

observations.period: June 1-15, 2026 survey; age, gender and income concentration

denominator.unit: U.S. investor subgroups; subgroup sample sizes are not disclosed in the article

younger_men_ownership.unit: percent of male investors aged 18-49 reporting cryptocurrency ownership

younger_men_ownership_2025.unit: percent of the same subgroup in 2025

upper_income_ownership.unit: percent of upper-income investors with household income of $90,000 or more

unequal_exposure.value: Crypto participation remains concentrated among younger men and higher-income investors even after broad ownership declines.

observations.method: Gallup subgroup comparisons among U.S. investors by age, gender and household income.
observations.uncertainty: The article does not disclose subgroup bases, weighting details or whether income differences reflect investable assets, risk capacity, access or demographic composition; concentration is not a causal exposure estimate.
observations.subgroup: Investors by age, gender and annual household income.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher-income investors may be better able to absorb volatility, while younger men may have greater exposure through social networks, platforms or risk-seeking financial cultures.

observations.period: June 1-15, 2026 survey; perceived investment risk and participation status

denominator.unit: U.S. investors; public article does not disclose the exact investor denominator

very_risky_overall.unit: percent of investors describing cryptocurrency as very risky

somewhat_risky_overall.unit: percent of investors describing it as somewhat risky

owner_very_risky.unit: percent of current cryptocurrency owners calling it very risky

intrigued_nonowner_very_risky.unit: percent of nonowners who are intrigued or plan to buy calling it very risky

uninterested_very_risky.unit: percent of investors uninterested in cryptocurrency calling it very risky

risk_participation_tension.value: Owners remain more likely than uninterested investors to describe crypto as risky, suggesting participation can coexist with explicit risk recognition.

observations.method: Gallup comparison of perceived cryptocurrency risk among owners, intrigued or intending nonowners, and uninterested investors.
observations.uncertainty: Risk perception is subjective and does not measure realized volatility, loss probability, financial harm or informed consent; the cross-sectional pattern cannot establish whether ownership changes risk beliefs.
observations.subgroup: U.S. investors by ownership and interest status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Owners may acknowledge risk because they have learned through exposure, or because they remain committed despite risk; nonowners may use risk language to rationalize nonparticipation.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-financial participation mechanism: crypto ownership has retreated from its 2025 peak while perceived risk remains high and participation stays concentrated among younger men and higher-income investors. It does not establish realized returns, losses, financial harm, suitability, debt, regulation, causal market behavior or durable cultural adoption.
